units.translation: where I restored θηρεύοντες [hunting] from the apograph for θηρεύσ θηρεύσοντες [hunting (future)]. For if Aeschylus had wanted to use the future, he would have written θηράσοντες [will hunt], since the tragedians do not seem to have said θηρεύειν [to hunt] for θηρᾶν [to hunt] except when the meter demanded it.
For ἐθηρεύθης [you were hunted] is corrupted from ὅθ᾽ ἡρέθης [when you were taken]. See αἱρέω [to take].
hunting marriages that are not to be hunted
faulty for θήρειον [wild beast], which see
there is for them a fountain of silver, a treasure of the earth
a choice gift to the children of Theseus
in a spurious verse invented to fill a lacuna, about which see what I said in the Preface to the fifth Leipzig edition p. XXI.
θιγεῖν [to touch] is an interpolation of Triclinius, about which see the annotation.
touching with their hands the blood of a bull
you speak again, touching the images
many things indeed touch the liver
touching with fearless hand and just touching
but for the one who touches there is no remedy from the bridal seats
and truly in battle she touched the hand of Zeus's daughter
whether it was a moray or a viper, touching it would have made another rot
about which see under the word ἐμβολή [embankment].
the embankments of the sea on the shore

(with perfect τέθνηκα [I have died], whose infinitive is τεθνηκέναι [to have died] or τεθνάναι [to have died], participle τεθνηκώς [having died] and τεθνεώς [having died], aorist ἔθανον [I died], future τεθνήξω [I will die] and θανοῦμαι [I will die]) to die.
The use of the participle is very frequent: θανών [having died], θανοῦσα [having died (fem.)], θανόν [having died (neut.)]
Genitive θανόντος [of the one who died], θανούσης [of the one who died (fem.)]
Dative θανόντι [to the one who died], θανούσῃ [to the one who died (fem.)]
Accusative θανόντα [the one who died], θανοῦσαν [the one who died (fem.)]
In the plural θανόντες [those who died], θανοῦσαι [those who died (fem.)]
Improperly of speech that is perishing

where M has θνάισκοντα [dying], with η written above by a second hand and ι deleted, in most apographs θνήσκοντα [dying]. (θνήσκω [I die] in M and in ancient codices of other writers and on inscriptions is not rarely written with iota adscript θνήισκω [I die], i.e. θνήσκω [I die], and similarly θρώισκω [I leap], i.e. θρώσκω [I leap], which Didymus disapproves in Etym. M. p. 452,30: about which Usener has spoken at greater length in Fleckeisen's Annals vol. 91 p. 245-247.)
where τεθνᾶναι [to have died] is faulty for τεθνάναι [to have died], with the middle syllable shortened. I corrected to χαίρω τι · τεθνᾶναι [I rejoice somewhat: to have died].
ἂν θάνοιεν [they might die] is faulty for ἀνθαλοῖεν [they might bloom again]. See ἀνθαλίσκομαι [to bloom again].
where Weil has ληφθέντες – θάνωσιν [having been taken – they might die].
nor does anyone die having received many wounds in his chest
he himself was present near the dying man
if you learn of men dying or wounded
where it is noble for the young to die
and to die dishonored and friendless by all
for thus you have not died
you have died, dearest might of Aegisthus
he has died shamefully, a cheat of money
